title: Boerner and Schulz (2009): Short-answer practice
instructions: Answer in English using a concise concept or number. Questions concern this 2009 article and the research it cites; diagnostic proposals are discussed in their historical context.

items.question: Which hypothesis predicts that caregiving strain and the subsequent death jointly deplete coping resources?
items.explanation: This perspective predicts greater adjustment difficulties after the loss. The authors consider it alongside relief and anticipation, with different combinations possible for different caregivers.

items.question: Which perspective predicts benefits when the death ends caregiving demands and the loved one's suffering?
items.explanation: Relief may coexist with exhaustion and mourning. It does not imply that the caregiver did not love or miss the person who died.

items.question: What process may help caregivers when they can consider the expected death and life afterwards before the loss occurs?
items.explanation: This is the third perspective discussed alongside depletion and relief. Expecting a death can provide opportunities to prepare, but does not guarantee preparedness in every domain.

items.question: In the authors' cited dementia-caregiver study, what percentage was at risk for clinical depression one year after the death?
items.explanation: The figure refers to risk in this particular study, not a universal rate of diagnosed depression. The same study reported complicated grief in 20%; a separate broader literature estimate of persistent difficulties was about 10–20%.

items.question: What feature of caregiver outcomes explains why no single perspective describes every person's adjustment?
items.explanation: Many caregivers improved, while a sizable minority continued to struggle. The authors argue that depletion, relief, and anticipation can apply to different subsets and can coexist.

items.question: What persistent and disruptive experience concerning the deceased was central to the grief criteria proposed in the literature discussed in this 2009 article?
items.explanation: The article describes a historical proposal that combined this experience with additional symptoms, duration, and impaired functioning. The question does not present those proposed criteria as current diagnostic rules.

items.question: Besides duration and symptoms, what impact on important life domains did the historical proposal require?
items.explanation: In the proposal described in this 2009 article, distress had to significantly impair important areas of life. The presence of sadness or the passage of time alone was insufficient under that proposal.

items.question: Which trauma-related disorder was named as potentially co-occurring with complicated grief?
items.explanation: The article also mentions major depression. Co-occurrence does not make these conditions interchangeable; the authors discuss distinct treatment approaches.

items.question: Which dimension of preparedness concerns being at peace with the prospect of death?
items.explanation: The cited focus-group work distinguishes this dimension from practical arrangements and medical information. Someone can be ready in those other areas while still feeling unprepared in this one.

items.question: Which dimension of preparedness includes arranging a funeral?
items.explanation: Concrete arrangements can be made without resolving emotional concerns. The dimensions should therefore be explored separately rather than treated as a single all-or-nothing state.

items.question: Which dimension of preparedness involves understanding medical aspects of the end of life?
items.explanation: Knowing what may happen medically is distinct from making arrangements or feeling emotionally ready. Even years of intensive caregiving do not ensure preparedness in all three dimensions.

items.question: What central source of purpose may be lost when caring for the person was a major source of meaning?
items.explanation: The authors offer this as one possible reason why positive caregiving experiences can accompany later bereavement difficulties. They also discuss losing a relationship that was central to the caregiver's life.

items.question: Which end-of-life support option does the article mention as a possible way to reduce caregiver burden?
items.explanation: The authors list this among options professionals might consider after discussing a caregiver's needs. It is not presented as the only option or as a guarantee of uncomplicated bereavement.

items.question: Which treatment component described in the cited study involves talking with the deceased in one's imagination?
items.explanation: The article lists this alongside retelling the death story and confronting avoided situations within a specialized treatment. It does not isolate this component as the sole cause of improvement.
items.source: A component of the cited treatment

items.question: Which standard depression treatment approach was the comparator in the cited Shear study?
items.explanation: As reported in this 2009 article, the specialized loss-focused approach produced higher and faster improvement in complicated grief than this comparator. That finding does not establish superiority for every condition or every person.
